key_terms.meaning: A calibrated oscillator, amplifier, attenuator and headphone set that presents pure tones of known frequency and known loudness to one ear at a time.
0 dB HL is the median threshold of hearing of healthy young ears at that frequency; a reading of 40 dB HL means the tone had to be 40 dB louder than normal.
Threshold search at octave or half-octave frequencies from 125 Hz to 8 kHz by the Hughson-Westlake method: 10 dB down after a response, 5 dB up after no response.
Tone delivered by a vibrator pressed on the mastoid, bypassing the outer and middle ear, so it tests the inner ear and nerve only.

Same machine, spoken words instead of tones: speech reception threshold is the level of 50 % correct word detection, and the discrimination score is the % of words repeated correctly at comfortable loudness.
A tube of fibres or a camera on a cable that carries light into a body cavity and an image back to the eye or a monitor.
A bundle in which the two ends are fused so that every fibre keeps the same place at both ends; only then is the pixel pattern of the image preserved.
Many unarranged glass fibres that only deliver illumination to the tip; order does not matter because no image travels through them.
The pointed lead-lined tube on a dental X-ray head that limits the beam to about 60 mm at the patient's skin.
Current that enters and leaves through the skin, so most of the voltage is dropped across the dry outer layer and the current is limited to milliamperes.
Current carried straight to the heart by a catheter, pacemaker lead or saline-filled tube, so skin resistance is bypassed and tens of microamperes are enough.

Current that flows from live parts to earth through insulation or capacitance rather than through the intended circuit; it is measured as the voltage across a 1 kΩ measuring device that stands in for the body.
Passing a known current (about 25 A) between the earth pin of the plug and exposed metal, and confirming the resistance is small (a fraction of an ohm).
Applying 500 V DC between live parts and the chassis or earth and confirming the resistance is very high (of the order of megohms), proving the insulation is dry and intact.
The band (A/B/C/D in India, I/IIa/IIb/III in Europe, I/II/III in the USA) that a regulator gives a device from its intended use and hazards; the class fixes the evidence and licence needed.
The transient fall in skin resistance that follows sweating after an arousing stimulus, recorded as a small wave on a chart.
The steady resistance of the skin at rest, mostly set by the moisture of the outer layer, typically in the hundreds of kilohms on the palm.
Instrument that measures eye pressure from the force needed to flatten a fixed area of cornea, using P = F/A.
A slit illuminator plus a stereo microscope that cuts an optical section through the transparent eye so each layer can be seen in depth.
Instrument that projects an infrared pattern onto the retina, measures the reflected image, and prints the sphere, cylinder and axis in dioptres.

takeaways: A pure-tone audiometer does one job: it finds the softest tone a person can hear at each frequency, and the answer is written in dB HL with 0 dB set to the normal ear.
The audiogram separates conductive loss from nerve loss by comparing air conduction with bone conduction; a gap between them means the outer or middle ear is at fault.
An endoscope needs one bundle to carry light in and a second, ordered bundle (or a camera chip) to carry the image out; if the image fibres lose their order, the picture becomes a blur of light.
A dental X-ray set uses low kVp, a small focal spot, a narrow collimator cone and a short exposure, so the dose per film is a few microsieverts.
Tissue is damaged by current, not by voltage; dry skin makes the body a poor conductor, but a catheter to the heart removes that protection.
Macroshock needs about 100 mA through the skin to fibrillate the heart, while microshock can do it with about 100 µA or less, which is why cardiac-connected equipment has the tightest leakage limits.
Electrical safety rests on three defences, earthing, isolation and double insulation, and is verified by four tests, inspection, earth continuity, insulation resistance and leakage current.
A device's risk class decides its regulatory path: the higher the class, the more bench data, animal or clinical evidence and third-party audit it needs before a licence.
A polygraph records skin resistance, breathing and pulse together and marks the moment of each question; it measures arousal, not truth, and courts treat it with caution.

Each ophthalmic instrument produces one number: the tonometer gives pressure in mmHg, the auto refractometer gives lens power in dioptres, and the slit lamp gives a magnified optical section rather than a number.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly 'principle, block diagram, working, specification, limitation', with the electrical safety question usually asked as a comparison of macroshock and microshock and the tests used to prove safety.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a pure-tone audiometer and explain how a hearing level in dB HL is defined, produced and plotted on an audiogram.
outline: Oscillator with frequency selection 125 Hz to 8 kHz
Amplifier, step attenuator in 5 dB steps, interrupter switch
Calibrated earphone and bone vibrator
0 dB HL = median threshold of normal ears, calibrated against reference equivalent threshold SPL
Audiogram: frequency on a log x-axis, dB HL on an inverted y-axis
Symbols O and X for right and left air conduction, < and > for bone conduction
Hughson-Westlake staircase procedure and masking of the non-test ear
answer: Purpose. A pure-tone audiometer finds the softest tone a person can hear at each frequency, one ear at a time, and records it as a hearing level in dB HL.

svg.aria: Block diagram of a pure-tone audiometer: oscillator from 125 hertz to 8 kilohertz, amplifier, attenuator in 5 decibel steps, interrupter switch, earphone or bone vibrator, and a patient response button, with a masking noise generator feeding the other ear.

answer.text: What each block does:

head: Block
Job
rows: sine wave at 125, 250, 500 Hz, 1, 2, 4, 8 kHz (and half-octaves)
raises the tone to drive the transducer
sets the level in 5 dB steps from about −10 to 120 dB HL
switches the tone on for 1–2 s with a soft rise and fall, so no click is heard
narrow-band noise to the non-test ear
air conduction through the whole ear; bone conduction through the skull to the inner ear

answer: How dB HL is defined. 0 dB HL at each frequency is the median threshold of healthy young ears. It is produced as a sound pressure, the reference equivalent threshold sound pressure level (RETSPL) of the earphone in use, which differs with frequency and earphone model, so the dial can be marked in dB HL for every frequency.

answer.text: Producing a level, at 1 kHz and 60 dB HL:
answer.pre:
insert earphone, RETSPL ≈ 0 dB SPL:  p = 20 µPa × 10<sup>60/20</sup> = 20 µPa × 1000 = 20 mPa
TDH-39 earphone, RETSPL 7 dB SPL:  67 dB SPL → p = 20 µPa × 10<sup>67/20</sup> = 44.8 mPa
one 5 dB attenuator step = pressure ratio 10<sup>5/20</sup> = 1.78

answer: Calibration. A coupler (artificial ear) and a sound-level meter check that each dial setting gives the right SPL; a daily listening check on a known ear catches faults between calibrations, and the earphone and audiometer are calibrated together.

answer.text: Plotting the audiogram:

head: Feature
Convention
rows: frequency, octave (logarithmic) spacing, 125 Hz to 8 kHz
dB HL, 0 at the top and larger numbers downward, so worse hearing plots lower
O right air, X left air, < right bone, > left bone

answer: Hughson–Westlake procedure. Start at 1 kHz, 30 dB HL. If not heard, go to 50 dB HL and up in 10 dB steps until heard. Then go down 10 dB after each response and up 5 dB after each miss; the threshold is the lowest level heard on two of three ascending runs. Test 2, 4, 8 kHz, retest 1 kHz, then 500 and 250 Hz.

Masking. A supra-aural tone crosses the skull about 40 dB weaker, so the non-test ear is masked with narrow-band noise when the test-ear air threshold is 40 dB or more above the non-test bone threshold, and for any bone-conduction test that shows an air-bone gap.
Closing check: 20 µPa × 10³ = 20 mPa; 60 + 7 = 67 dB SPL gives 44.8 mPa; 10<sup>0.25</sup> = 1.78 per 5 dB step.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a flexible fibre-optic endoscope. Explain why the image bundle must be coherent while the light bundle need not be.
outline: Two bundles: light guide and image guide
Core and cladding of each fibre, total internal reflection
Fibre diameter of the order of 10 to 30 micrometres; thousands of fibres
Objective lens at the tip, eyepiece or camera coupler at the other end
Coherent bundle keeps the same fibre order at both ends, so it carries a pixel map of the image
Incoherent bundle only delivers light to the cavity
Air and water channels, bending section, deflection controls, light source and insufflation
answer: Purpose. A flexible endoscope carries light into a body cavity and an image back out along a bending shaft, so the stomach, colon or bronchi can be seen through a natural opening.

svg.aria: Light path of a flexible endoscope: a lamp outside the body feeds the incoherent light guide to the tip, the objective lens focuses the tissue onto the coherent image guide of 10 000 fibres, and the eyepiece or camera shows the picture.

answer.text: Total internal reflection in one fibre. Each fibre has a core of index n₁ = 1.50 inside a cladding of n₂ = 1.47:
answer.pre:
sin θc = n₂ / n₁ = 1.47 / 1.50 = 0.98 → θc = 78.5° from the normal
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √(2.250 − 2.161) = √0.0891 = 0.30
acceptance half-angle in air = sin⁻¹ 0.30 = 17.4°

answer: Rays that enter within 17.4° of the axis strike the wall beyond the critical angle and are reflected again and again without loss, even when the fibre bends gently.

answer.text: The two bundles:

head: Light guide
Image guide
rows: coherent: each fibre in the same place at both ends, ends fused and polished
carry the picture point by point

answer: Why the image bundle must be coherent. The objective lens forms an image on the bundle face; each fibre carries the brightness of one small spot, like one pixel. Only if fibre k sits in the same place at the eyepiece end is that pixel shown in the right place. The light guide carries no picture, so its order does not matter.

answer.text: Numbers for a 10 000-fibre image bundle with 30 µm cores:
answer.pre:
one core: π × (15 µm)² = 707 µm²
all cores: 10 000 × 707 µm² = 7.07 × 10⁶ µm² = 7.07 mm²
resolution: about one fibre spacing (core + cladding), a little over 30 µm

answer.text: Other parts:

head: Part
Job
rows: focuses the tissue onto the image bundle face
magnifies the bundle face for the eye or a camera
two pairs of cables pulled by knobs at the handle steer the tip up, down, left and right
insufflate the cavity and wash the lens
xenon or LED lamp, with the heat kept outside the body

answer: Care. Flexible scopes cannot be autoclaved; they are leak-tested, cleaned and disinfected chemically between patients.

bank.q: Explain macroshock and microshock. Give the current thresholds for perception, let-go, respiratory tetany and ventricular fibrillation, and state the leakage limits for cardiac-connected equipment.
outline: Injury depends on current density and path, not on voltage
Body resistance: dry skin about 10 to 100 kilohm, internal tissue a few hundred ohm
Perception about 1 mA, let-go about 10 to 16 mA, respiratory tetany 20 to 30 mA, fibrillation 75 to 100 mA at 50 Hz
Microshock: conductor inside the heart, skin resistance bypassed, fibrillation possible at tens of microamperes
Microshock pathways: saline-filled catheter, pacemaker lead, wet electrode, earthed plumbing
Limits: patient leakage 10 µA for type CF and 100 µA for type BF; enclosure leakage 100 µA; earth leakage 5 mA in the current standard (0.5 mA in older editions)
answer: Principle. Injury depends on the current through the body, its path and its duration, not on the voltage. The voltage only decides how much current a given resistance lets through, I = V ÷ R.

answer.text: Body resistance:

head: Path
Resistance
rows: Dry intact skin, hand to hand

answer.text: Macroshock: current enters and leaves through the skin. Effects at 50 Hz for about 1 s, hand to hand:

head: Current
Effect
rows: let-go: the hand cannot release the conductor
respiratory tetany: breathing stops while the current flows

answer.text: Worked numbers at 230 V:
answer.pre:
dry skin 10 kΩ: I = 230 / 10 000 = 23 mA → above let-go, below fibrillation
wet skin 1 kΩ:  I = 230 / 1000  = 230 mA → 2.3 × the 100 mA fibrillation level

answer: Microshock: a conductor inside the heart (saline-filled catheter, pacing wire, guide wire) carries current straight to the myocardium. Skin resistance is bypassed and the current is concentrated on a small patch of muscle, so about 100 µA, in some studies 20 µA, can fibrillate the heart.

answer.text: Microshock numbers:
answer.pre:
catheter path 500 Ω, 0.1 V offset: I = 0.1 / 500 = 200 µA
200 µA is 20 × the 10 µA limit and above the ≈ 100 µA fibrillation level
100 mA / 20 µA = 5000: the danger levels differ by thousands

answer: Microshock pathways: a saline-filled catheter or pacing wire touched by a hand that also touches an earthed bed; leakage from a mains-powered device into a CF applied part; a wet electrode; earthed plumbing near the patient.

Why 50 Hz is worst: nerve and muscle are most easily excited by alternating current in the tens of hertz, and a shock that lasts over the T wave (the vulnerable period) is most likely to start fibrillation.

answer.text: Leakage limits (IEC 60601-1):

head: Current
Normal condition
Single fault
rows: Patient leakage, type B or BF

answer: The 10 µA CF limit is ten times below the ≈ 100 µA microshock level, a safety factor for an unknown patient and path.
Closing check: 230 / 10 kΩ = 23 mA; 230 / 1 kΩ = 230 mA; 0.1 V / 500 Ω = 200 µA.

bank.q: List and explain the four tests used to verify the electrical safety of a medical equipment installation.
outline: Visual inspection: plug, cord, fuse rating, labels, battery, no cracks
Earth continuity: about 25 A injected between earth pin and exposed metal, resistance well under 1 ohm
Insulation resistance: 500 V DC between live parts and chassis or earth, resistance in the megohm range
Leakage current: equipment connected to supply with the leads in a safety analyser, earth leakage, enclosure leakage and patient leakage measured in normal and single-fault condition
Accept and reject values with reference to the applicable standard
Records and repeat test intervals
answer: Purpose. The tests prove that the three defences work: the protective earth, the insulation, and the limits on leakage. They are done on delivery, after any repair, and at set intervals (often yearly, more often in critical areas), and every result is recorded.

svg.aria: Six steps of an electrical safety test: visual inspection, earth continuity at about 25 amperes with a limit of 0.1 to 0.3 ohm, insulation resistance at 500 volts with at least 1 megohm, leakage in normal condition, leakage in single fault with earth or neutral open, and a functional test.

answer: Test 1: visual inspection (device unplugged). Check the plug, cord and strain relief, the fuse rating against the label, the labels and applied-part symbols, cracks, liquid ingress, batteries and accessories. Many faults are found here before any meter is used.

answer.text: Test 2: earth continuity. A test current of about 25 A (or at least 0.2 A on many analysers) is passed from the earth pin to exposed metal; the resistance is read:
answer.pre:
limit ≈ 0.1 Ω (0.2 Ω with a detachable cord; 0.3 Ω in many routine procedures)
25 A through 0.1 Ω drops only 2.5 V
worked case: 0.35 Ω → FAIL

answer: A high current is used so that a single surviving strand of a broken earth wire, which would pass a small test current, overheats or shows its true resistance.

answer.text: Test 3: insulation resistance. 500 V DC between the joined live and neutral and the earthed metal:
answer.pre:
limit ≥ 1 MΩ (many procedures ask 2 MΩ)
at the limit the test current is 500 V / 1 MΩ = 0.5 mA
worked case: 50 MΩ → PASS

answer: Test 4: leakage current (device running, plugged into the analyser). Earth leakage, enclosure (touch) leakage and patient leakage from each applied part are measured through the 1 kΩ measuring device, first in normal condition, then in single fault with the protective earth opened and then the neutral opened.

answer.text: Accept and reject values:
Worked ventilator result:
answer.pre:
earth 0.35 Ω > 0.1 Ω → FAIL
insulation 50 MΩ ≥ 1 MΩ → pass
earth leakage 0.9 mA ≤ 5 mA → pass
action: withdraw, repair the earth path, repeat every test

answer: Records and intervals. Record the asset number, date, readings, limits, analyser serial number and tester; label the device with the next test date. Any failure takes the device out of service until it is repaired and retested.
Closing check: 25 A × 0.1 Ω = 2.5 V; 500 V / 1 MΩ = 0.5 mA; 0.35 > 0.1 fails.

bank.q: Explain how a polygraph records galvanic skin response, respiration and pulse. Define basal skin resistance and say why all channels are recorded together.
outline: GSR: two electrodes on palm or fingers, a small constant current or voltage, resistance or conductance recorded
Basal skin resistance is the resting value, hundreds of kilohm on the palm
An arousing stimulus triggers sweat secretion and resistance falls, giving a wave
Respiration by a chest and an abdominal belt, pneumograph or strain gauge
Cardiovascular channel by cuff or photoplethysmograph
Marker pen or digital event mark at the instant each question is asked
Why together: arousal appears in several channels at different delays, and the marker separates stimulus from response
answer: Purpose. A polygraph records several signals of autonomic arousal on one time base and marks the instant each question is asked, so each response can be matched to its question.

answer.text: Channels:

head: Channel
Sensor
What changes with arousal
rows: two Ag/AgCl electrodes on palm or fingers, constant current
pneumograph belts on chest and abdomen (strain gauge or bellows)
arm cuff at low pressure, or a finger photoplethysmograph
pulse rate and blood pressure rise
shows the moment of each question

answer: Basal skin resistance (BSR) is the resting resistance between the two electrodes, set by the moisture of the outer skin: tens of kilohms to about a megohm, often hundreds of kilohms on a dry palm. The GSR is the transient fall from BSR after a stimulus, as sympathetic nerves fill the sweat ducts with salty, conducting sweat.

answer.text: How the GSR is measured (constant current 10 µA):
answer.pre:
rest: V = 1.5 V → BSR = 1.5 / 10 µA = 150 kΩ (G = 6.67 µS)
after the question: V = 1.2 V → R = 120 kΩ (G = 8.33 µS)
fall 30 kΩ = 20 %; conductance response 1.67 µS = 25 %

answer: The current is kept small (around 10 µA) so it does not stimulate or polarise; a bridge balanced at BSR can be used instead, with the out-of-balance voltage as the GSR. Because the meter reads voltage, a fall in resistance shows as a fall in voltage.
Respiration. Each belt converts the change in girth into a voltage; the trace shows rate and depth, and a breath hold shows as a flat stretch.
Pulse. A cuff inflated to about 60 mmHg follows the pressure pulse; a photoplethysmograph follows the blood volume in the finger. Both show rate and relative pressure changes.

answer.text: Why all channels are recorded together:

head: Reason
Explanation
rows: breathing changes within the next breath, pulse within a few beats, GSR after 1–3 s; a common time base lines them up
one channel alone can change from a cough or movement; arousal shows as a pattern across channels
a deep breath or movement seen on one channel explains a GSR wave on another
the marker separates the question from the response, so latency can be measured

answer: Signal conditioning. Each channel has its own amplifier and filter; the GSR channel has a baseline control so the slow BSR drift can be offset, and all channels are written by one recorder or computer.

bank.q: An audiogram shows air conduction of 40 dB HL and bone conduction of 10 dB HL at 2 kHz in one ear, with normal readings at 250 Hz. Interpret the result, name the type of loss and state where the defect lies.
outline: Air-bone gap of 30 dB at 2 kHz
Bone conduction near normal means the inner ear and nerve work
Gap means the outer or middle ear blocks air-conducted sound
Diagnosis: conductive hearing loss, here mild to moderate at 2 kHz
Possible causes: wax, effusion, otosclerosis, perforation
Next steps: otoscopy, tympanometry, repeat with masking to rule out cross-hearing
answer: Data. Right or left ear at 2 kHz: air conduction 40 dB HL, bone conduction 10 dB HL; at 250 Hz normal readings for both.

answer.text: Air-bone gap:
answer.pre:
gap = AC − BC = 40 − 10 = 30 dB at 2 kHz
BC 10 dB HL is within the normal 0–20 dB HL

answer: Bone conduction near normal means the cochlea and the auditory nerve respond normally when sound reaches them directly through the skull. So the inner ear and nerve work.
The 30 dB gap means air-conducted sound loses 30 dB on the way to the cochlea: the block is in the outer ear (canal) or the middle ear (drum, ossicles, middle-ear space).

answer.text: Type and degree:

head: Feature
Finding
rows: conductive hearing loss (gap over 10 dB with normal bone)
40 dB HL: mild, at the border of moderate (26–40 mild, 41–55 moderate)
normal at 250 Hz, loss at 2 kHz: a localised, not a flat, loss

answer.text: How it would look on the audiogram:
answer.pre:
2 kHz:  O (or X) at 40 dB HL, < (or >) at 10 dB HL
        30 dB vertical gap between the bone and air symbols
250 Hz: both symbols near 0–20 dB HL

answer.text: Possible causes:

head: Cause
Clue
rows: fixed stapes; often a dip in bone conduction near 2 kHz (Carhart notch)

answer: A high-frequency-only conductive loss with normal low frequencies is unusual, so the result should be confirmed: a mass-type problem (for example ossicular) or a test error can give it.

Masking check. Interaural attenuation for bone conduction is about 0 dB, so an unmasked bone threshold may come from the other cochlea. The bone threshold must be repeated with narrow-band masking noise in the non-test ear before the gap is accepted.

Next steps: otoscopy, tympanometry and acoustic reflexes, repeat audiometry with masking, then refer to an ENT surgeon; treat the cause (wax removal, management of effusion, surgery for otosclerosis).

answer.text: How the other types would differ at the same frequency:

answer: Closing check: 40 − 10 = 30 dB gap; bone 10 dB HL is normal, so the loss is conductive.

bank.q: A technician tests a Class I patient monitor in an ICU and records earth continuity of 0.8 ohm, insulation resistance of 0.5 megohm and earth leakage current of 300 microampere. Decide which results pass, and state what protection a patient with a pacemaker needs.
outline: Earth continuity 0.8 Ω is above the 0.1–0.3 Ω allowed for a protective earth, so this fails
Insulation resistance 0.5 MΩ is below the 1 MΩ minimum (many procedures ask 2 MΩ), so this fails
Earth leakage 300 µA is well under the 5 mA limit (and the older 500 µA limit), so it passes
Any single failure means the unit is withdrawn and repaired
Pacemaker patient needs type CF, cardiac-floating, applied part
Patient leakage limit about 10 microampere; isolated input, battery operation where possible
Equipotential bonding, no unearthed metal near the bed, earth-free zone for intracardiac procedures

answer.text: Results against the limits:

answer: Earth continuity. 0.8 Ω means a loose terminal, corroded pin or broken strands. If live touches the case, the fault current through 0.8 Ω may not blow the fuse quickly, and the case rises toward mains voltage.

answer.text: What 0.8 Ω means in a fault (230 V supply, 0.4 Ω of supply wiring):
answer.pre:
fault current ≈ 230 / (0.4 + 0.8) = 192 A → most of the time the fuse blows
case voltage ≈ 192 A × 0.8 Ω = 153 V until it does
with a good 0.1 Ω earth: 230 / 0.5 = 460 A, case at 46 V, fuse blows at once

answer.text: Insulation resistance. 0.5 MΩ shows damp, dirty or damaged insulation:
answer.pre:
at 230 V: 230 / 0.5 MΩ = 460 µA flows through the insulation to the case
with a broken earth, that current would pass through anyone touching the case

answer.text: Earth leakage. 300 µA passes the 5 mA limit, but it matters if the earth is lost:
answer.pre:
300 µA through a nurse touching the case and a pacing wire
= 3 × the ≈ 100 µA microshock level, 30 × the 10 µA CF limit

answer: Decision. Any single failure means the monitor is labelled out of service, repaired (earth path, insulation), and the full test sequence repeated before it returns to the ICU. A monitor cannot be "mostly safe".

answer.text: Protection for a patient with a pacemaker (especially a temporary external pacing wire):

head: Measure
Why
rows: Type CF applied parts on every connected device
Isolated patient inputs (isolation transformer, optocoupler) or battery operation
no mains path to the patient
Equipotential bonding of all metal near the bed
no voltage difference between things a person can touch
Earth-free zone: no unearthed or separately earthed metal within reach
no second path to complete a circuit through the heart
Insulated, capped pacing-wire terminals; gloves when handling them
no hand contact with the wire
monitor survives a shock and recovers

answer: Record keeping. Write the readings, the limits, the analyser used and the date on the test sheet and on the asset label, so the repair and the retest can be compared with this result.
Closing check: 0.8 > 0.1 Ω fails; 0.5 < 1 MΩ fails; 300 µA < 5 mA passes; 300 µA is 30 × 10 µA.

bank.q: Describe a dental X-ray machine and list the practical steps that keep the patient's dose low during an intraoral exposure.
outline: Tube: tungsten anode, thermionic filament, evacuated glass envelope, oil and lead housing
Settings of the order of 60 to 70 kVp and a few milliampere, exposure of a fraction of a second
Small focal spot, short cone or open-ended spacer, collimation to about 60 mm at the skin
Aluminium filtration to remove soft X-rays

Steps: correct film or sensor, fast film or digital, lead apron and thyroid collar, beam-aiming with the patient still, avoid retakes, hold film by holder not by finger, staff behind shield, badge monitoring
Dose per intraoral film is a few microsieverts; ALARA principle

answer.text: Construction of the tube head:

head: Part
Detail
rows: heated tungsten coil, emits electrons; its current sets the tube mA
stationary tungsten insert in a copper block; focal spot under 1 mm
lead-lined head filled with insulating oil, one beam window
step-up transformer, often self-rectified; or a high-frequency inverter
1.5 mm Al total at 70 kVp or below, 2.5 mm above
sets focus-to-skin distance (≥ 20 cm above 60 kVp) and beam ≤ 6 cm at the skin
electronic, 0.01 s steps, dead-man switch on a long cord

answer.text: Settings and what they give (70 kVp, 7 mA, 0.6 s):
answer.pre:
exposure = 7 mA × 0.6 s = 4.2 mAs
highest photon energy 70 keV;  λmin = 1.24 / 70 = 0.0177 nm
electrical energy ≈ 70 kV × 7 mA × 0.6 s = 294 J; X-rays 0.57 % = 1.7 J; heat 292 J

answer: kVp sets the penetration and contrast; mA × s sets the number of photons and so the film blackening and the dose.

answer.text: Why the cone length matters (inverse square):
answer.pre:
20 cm → 40 cm: dose at the skin × (20/40)² = 1/4
20 cm → 30 cm: × (20/30)² = 0.44
longer cone: more parallel rays, less magnification

answer.text: Practical steps that keep the dose low:

head: Step
Effect
rows: Fastest receptor: E/F film or digital sensor
less mAs for the same image
Rectangular collimation to the sensor size
Long cone, correct kVp, aluminium filtration
less skin dose from soft X-rays
no fingers in the beam, fewer retakes
Patient still, correct angle, correct exposure
avoid retakes, which double the dose
Operator 2 m away, out of the beam or behind a screen, with a dose badge
staff dose kept low and monitored
no exposure without a clinical reason

answer: Dose per film. A single intraoral exposure gives an effective dose of a few microsieverts, roughly a day of natural background radiation; the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable) still applies because every exposure carries a small risk.
Quality assurance. Check timer accuracy, kVp and the beam size each year, and the processing or sensor at set intervals, so the chosen exposure gives the intended image.

bank.q: An auto refractometer prints -2.00 D sphere, -0.75 D cylinder, axis 180 degrees for the right eye. Explain what each number means and how the instrument obtained them.
outline: Dioptre is the reciprocal of focal length in metres
Negative sphere means myopia, the eye is too powerful or too long
Cylinder is the extra power in one meridian, axis is its direction in degrees
Instrument projects an infrared ring or pattern onto the retina and measures the size and shape of the reflected image
Spherical error shifts focus, astigmatism distorts the image into an ellipse
Internal computation averages several readings and gives vertex distance and pupillary distance
Purpose: quick objective starting point before subjective refraction
answer: The numbers. −2.00 DS / −0.75 DC × 180 means sphere −2.00 dioptres, cylinder −0.75 dioptres with its axis at 180°.

answer.text: Dioptre. Power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres:
answer.pre: F = 1 / f;  −2.00 D → f = −0.50 m (a diverging lens)

answer: Negative sphere means myopia: the eye is too powerful for its length, so distant light focuses in front of the retina; a minus lens spreads the rays so they focus on it.
Cylinder and axis. The cylinder adds power in one meridian only. Its axis is the meridian where it has no power; its power acts at 90° to the axis.

answer.text: Working out the two meridians:
answer.pre:
180° meridian: sphere only = −2.00 D → far point 1/2.00 = 0.50 m
 90° meridian: −2.00 + (−0.75) = −2.75 D → far point 1/2.75 = 0.36 m
spherical equivalent = −2.00 + (−0.75/2) = −2.38 D
same lens in plus-cylinder form: −2.75 DS / +0.75 DC × 90

answer: So vertical and horizontal lines blur at different distances: this is regular astigmatism, with the rule (minus-cylinder axis near 180°).

answer.text: How the instrument obtained the numbers:

head: Stage
What happens
rows: the patient looks at a target that is moved slightly beyond focus, so accommodation relaxes
an invisible IR ring or pattern (about 850 nm) is sent through the pupil onto the retina; the pupil stays wide
light returning through the eye's optics is imaged onto a sensor
a spherical error changes the size or focus of the ring; astigmatism turns the ring into an ellipse whose axes give the cylinder axis (or a Shack–Hartmann lenslet array shifts its spots)
several readings averaged; printed for a vertex distance of usually 12 mm, often with the pupillary distance

answer: Purpose and limits. The reading is objective and fast, so it is used in busy clinics, screening and for children, but it is only a starting point: subjective refraction with trial lenses and a chart refines it, because accommodation, small pupils and media opacities can bias the machine.

answer.text: If the patient wants contact lenses, each meridian is moved from the 12 mm spectacle plane to the cornea:
answer.pre:
Fc = F / (1 − d F),  d = 0.012 m
180°: −2.00 / (1 + 0.024) = −1.95 D
 90°: −2.75 / (1 + 0.033) = −2.66 D
contact-lens cylinder ≈ −0.71 D, so a little less minus power is needed

bank.q: Compare the electrical safety design of an ECG machine used in a general ward with one used in a cardiac catheterisation laboratory. Justify each difference.
outline: Ward: intact skin, macroshock is the main risk, type BF or Class I with protective earth is acceptable
Cath lab: catheter or guide wire inside the heart, microshock dominates
Type CF applied part, patient leakage current of the order of 10 microampere
Isolation of the patient circuit by transformer, optocoupler or battery operation
Earth-free zone or equipotential bonding of all metal near the table
Single-fault condition testing, no earthed metal within reach of the patient
Defibrillation-proof inputs because a defibrillator is used in the same room
answer: The difference in one line. On a ward the ECG electrodes sit on intact skin, so macroshock is the risk; in a catheterisation laboratory a catheter or guide wire is inside the heart, so microshock dominates and every limit tightens.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
General ward ECG
Cath-lab ECG
Why
rows: heart contact needs the cardiac-floating limit
isolation transformer or optocoupler essential, or battery
no mains path through the catheter
class I with equipotential bonding of all metal near the table
no voltage difference between touchable parts
essential: defibrillator used in the same room
shorter interval, single-fault tests on every applied part

answer.text: Why the CF limit is ten times lower:
answer.pre:
skin path, 230 V on wet skin 1 kΩ → 230 mA (macroshock needs ≈ 100 mA)
catheter path 500 Ω, 0.1 V → 200 µA (microshock needs ≈ 100 µA)
CF 10 µA leaves a safety factor of 10 below 100 µA

answer: Isolation. The patient circuit of a CF monitor floats: an isolation amplifier (transformer or optical coupling) separates it from the mains-referenced circuits, with very small capacitance across the barrier, so even with a fault the current through the patient stays below 50 µA.

Equipotential bonding. In the cath lab every metal part within reach of the patient (table, monitor cases, infusion stands, pipes) is bonded to one earth point with low-resistance bonding conductors, so a person touching two metal parts and a catheter cannot drive current through the heart.
Earth-free practice. Staff handle catheters and pacing wires with gloved hands, avoid touching earthed metal at the same time, and use insulated covers on exposed connectors.

answer.text: Defibrillation protection, as in the ward but more critical:
answer.pre: two 20 kΩ series resistors: 5000 V / 40 kΩ = 125 mA, neon shunt at 60–100 V, clamp diodes

answer: Ward. A BF monitor with a good protective earth, routine testing and the usual electrode care is enough because the skin and tissue limit any fault current to the milliampere range and the threshold there is about 100 mA.
Closing check: 0.1 V / 500 Ω = 200 µA > 100 µA; 10 µA is one-tenth of 100 µA; 5000 / 40 000 = 0.125 A.

bank.q: A start-up has built a new pulse oximeter. Trace the route from working prototype to legal sale in India, and explain how a change of risk class changes the evidence demanded.
outline: Fix the intended use and the risk class under the national medical device rules, class A to D in India
Quality management system, generally ISO 13485, and risk management to ISO 14971
Bench tests: electrical safety to IEC 60601-1 and its particular standard, electromagnetic compatibility, performance and accuracy of SpO2
Biocompatibility of the sensor, software validation, shelf life and sterilisation if applicable
Clinical evidence or literature for the claims, more for higher classes

A pulse oximeter is class B, so the manufacturing licence comes from the State Licensing Authority after a notified-body audit; class C or D would go to the Central Licensing Authority; then labelling and unique device identification
Post-market surveillance, complaint handling and adverse event reporting, and re-evaluation if the intended use widens into a higher class

answer.text: Step 1: fix the intended use and the risk class. A spot-check pulse oximeter that measures SpO₂ and pulse rate through the finger skin is an active, non-invasive diagnostic device:
answer.pre:
Indian class: B (low–moderate risk) → manufacturing licence from the State Licensing Authority
if the claim widens to continuous monitoring with alarms in critical care → class C → Central Licensing Authority

answer: Step 2: quality management system to ISO 13485 (design control, supplier control, production, records) and risk management to ISO 14971 (hazards such as wrong reading, skin burn, electric shock, alarm failure; risk controls; residual risk).

answer.text: Step 3: bench tests:

head: Test
Standard or purpose
rows: ISO 80601-2-61: SpO₂ accuracy, pulse rate, alarms

answer.text: Accuracy is stated as A<sub>rms</sub>, the root-mean-square difference from arterial blood-gas SpO₂. For five paired readings with errors +2, −1, +3, −2 and +1 %:
answer.pre:
A<sub>rms</sub> = √[(4 + 1 + 9 + 4 + 1) / 5] = √3.8 = 1.95 %
limit: ≤ 4 % in the standard (many regulators expect ≤ 3 %) → pass

answer: A real study uses many subjects and readings over 70–100 % saturation, with a range of skin pigmentation, because pigmentation can bias optical readings.

Step 4: clinical evidence. For class B, bench data plus a desaturation study or published equivalence may suffice; class C or D needs a stronger clinical evaluation and often a clinical investigation.

Step 5: licence. Prepare the device master file and plant master file, apply to the licensing authority for the class, pass the audit of the manufacturing site (by a notified body for class A and B, by the central authority for C and D), and receive the manufacturing licence. Label with intended use, warnings, batch and unique device identification.

answer.text: How a change of class changes the evidence:

head: Class B
Class C or D
rows: full clinical evaluation, often an investigation
tighter surveillance and periodic safety reports

answer: Step 6: post-market surveillance. Collect complaints, report serious adverse events to the regulator, trend field data, issue field safety corrections, and re-classify and re-submit if the intended use widens.
Closing check: √3.8 = 1.95 % ≤ 3 %; class B goes to the State authority, class C or D to the Central authority.

bank.q: A polygraph record shows a large GSR wave to the fourth question, no change in breathing and a small rise in pulse. Evaluate how much weight this deserves and identify the sources of error.
outline: Polygraph measures arousal, not deception
GSR is the most sensitive and fastest channel but also the least specific
Single channel response has no diagnostic value on its own
Order effects and habituation; the question before may carry over
Artefacts: movement, deep breath, cough, dry electrodes, loose cuff, room temperature, sweat from fear of the test itself
Countermeasures by the subject: biting the tongue, tensing muscles, mental arithmetic
Legal position in India: results without consent are not admissible as evidence; consent and expert interpretation needed
answer: The record. Question 4 produced a large GSR wave, no change in breathing and a small rise in pulse. The question is how much this deserves to be believed as a sign of deception.

What the polygraph measures. It records arousal of the sympathetic nervous system: sweating, breathing and pulse. Arousal comes from guilt, but equally from fear of the test, anger, embarrassment, surprise or a painful memory. It does not measure truth.

answer.text: Reading the channels:

head: Channel
Finding
Weight
rows: most sensitive and fastest-recovering marker, but the least specific
no supporting breath hold or suppression

answer.text: Checking it is a real GSR rather than an artefact (constant current 10 µA):
answer.pre:
baseline 1.5 V → 150 kΩ;  dip to 1.2 V → 120 kΩ (20 % fall, 1.67 µS)
a true response starts 1–3 s after the question mark and recovers over several seconds
a dip that starts before the mark, or with a movement, is an artefact

answer.text: Sources of error:

head: Source
Example
rows: carry-over from question 3; the first relevant question often gives the biggest response
responses shrink with repetition, so a fourth-question response is not comparable with the first
movement, cough, deep breath, loose cuff or belt, dry or shifted electrodes, room temperature
fear of the test itself, illness, drugs, fatigue
tongue biting, tensing muscles, mental arithmetic on control questions

answer: Evaluation. A single-channel response to a single question has no diagnostic value on its own. The question should be repeated in a different order, compared with control questions, and judged only if the reaction repeats across channels and presentations.

Legal position in India. In 2010 the Supreme Court held that polygraph, narco-analysis and brain-mapping tests cannot be given without the person's consent, and that the results themselves cannot be treated as evidence; only facts discovered as a result of a voluntary test may be used, and expert interpretation is needed.
Conclusion. The record shows arousal at question 4, nothing more. It deserves little weight: at most a lead for further enquiry, never proof.

bank.q: Compare Goldmann applanation tonometry with Schiotz indentation tonometry, and state which is preferred for a mass glaucoma screening camp and why.
outline: Both use force over an area; normal intraocular pressure is roughly 10 to 21 mmHg
Goldmann: flattens a fixed 3.06 mm diameter area, force read with a slit lamp, fluorescein and cobalt blue light, Imbert-Fick assumption
Schiotz: weighted plunger indents the cornea, deflection read on a scale and converted by a calibration chart
Goldmann: more accurate, less affected by corneal stiffness, needs slit lamp, anaesthetic and trained operator
Schiotz: portable and cheap but dependent on corneal rigidity and calibration
Screening choice: non-contact air-puff or portable rebound tonometer when many people must be seen quickly, with abnormal cases referred for Goldmann
Confounders: corneal thickness, astigmatism, pressure on the lid
answer: Common basis. Both estimate intra-ocular pressure from the force needed to deform the cornea; normal IOP is about 10–21 mmHg.

answer.text: Goldmann applanation. A prism on the slit lamp flattens a fixed circle of 3.06 mm diameter (Imbert–Fick, P = F/A):

answer: At 3.06 mm the corneal stiffness pushing out and the tear-film surface tension pulling in cancel, so the flat area really reflects the fluid pressure. The cornea is anaesthetised and stained with fluorescein; in cobalt-blue light two green semicircles are seen and the knob is turned until their inner edges just touch.

Schiotz indentation. A plunger carrying a known weight (5.5 g, with 7.5 g and 10 g added for high pressures) rests on the anaesthetised cornea of a lying patient. The softer the eye, the deeper the plunger sinks; the scale reading is converted to mmHg with a calibration table for that weight. A higher reading means a lower pressure.

Schiotz indentation

about 0.5 µL, so it hardly raises the pressure

answer.text: Confounders for both:
answer.pre:
thick cornea reads high, thin cornea reads low
high astigmatism distorts the mires (Goldmann)
pressure on the lids or a squeezing patient raises the reading

answer.text: Mass screening camp, about 300 people in a day:
answer.pre:
Goldmann: about 3–5 min each with drops and staining → 15–25 h of examiner time
non-contact or rebound tonometer: about 1 min each → about 5 h, no drops, no contact

answer: Choice. Neither Goldmann nor Schiotz is ideal for screening. A non-contact air-puff tonometer or a hand-held rebound tonometer is preferred: quick, no anaesthetic, no fluorescein, lower infection risk and usable by a trained technician. Anyone above about 21 mmHg, or with a suspicious optic disc, is referred for Goldmann applanation, the reference measurement. Where only basic equipment exists, Schiotz is acceptable as a cheap portable screen, with the same referral rule.

glossary.def: A graph of hearing threshold in dB HL against frequency in hertz, drawn separately for each ear.
The difference in dB between air-conduction and bone-conduction thresholds at one frequency; a gap points to a conductive loss.
A noise presented to the non-test ear so that a loud tone in the test ear is not heard by the other cochlea.
Light travelling in a fibre core strikes the cladding at a shallow angle and is reflected back completely, so it stays inside the fibre.
The hollow tube running the length of a flexible endoscope through which biopsy forceps, snares or suction are passed.
An endoscope with a small solid-state camera chip at the tip instead of an image bundle, sending a video signal up the cable.
The small area on the X-ray anode where electrons strike and X-rays are produced; a smaller spot gives a sharper image.
Peak kilovoltage across an X-ray tube, which decides the penetrating power of the beam.
As low as reasonably achievable, the rule that every radiation exposure is kept to the minimum that still gives the needed information.
The largest current at which a person can still release a gripped conductor, about 10 to 16 mA at mains frequency.
Chaotic uncoordinated contraction of the heart muscle, fatal within minutes without defibrillation, and the main electrical hazard of shock.
Current that flows from the applied part of equipment through the patient to earth, measured under normal and single-fault conditions.
A cardiac-floating applied part, isolated from earth and from other circuits so that it is safe for direct connection to the heart.
Equipment protected by basic insulation plus a protective earth conductor connected to exposed metal.
Basic insulation plus supplementary insulation with no reliance on earth, used in Class II equipment.
A transformer whose primary and secondary are not electrically connected, used to break the path from mains earth to the patient.
A breaker that trips when the current in the live wire and the neutral wire differ by a small set value, indicating current is leaking to earth.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, the Indian authority that licenses medical devices and sets their risk classes.
The international standard for a quality management system in the design and manufacture of medical devices.
A regulatory submission, commonly called 510(k) in the United States, showing a moderate-risk device is substantially equivalent to one already on the market.
The reciprocal of skin resistance, measured in microsiemens and preferred in modern work because it varies more linearly with sweat gland activity.
The fluid pressure inside the eyeball, normally about 10 to 21 mmHg, raised in glaucoma.
The unit of lens power, equal to the reciprocal of the focal length in metres; a 2 D lens focuses parallel light at 0.5 m.
Measurement of the curvature of the front surface of the cornea, usually given as the radius in millimetres and power in dioptres in two meridians.
